vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: strong enough for a court to make you keep it
to make somebody follow a rule or a contract
to reach a senior position step by step, from inside
the country or the court whose law decides a case
to give the final approval to something
one numbered part of a contract that says one thing
everything a person has done before, seen as proof
the moment when somebody does not do what the contract says

items.situation: Martin asks: "How long have you worked in agribusiness?"
tips: I have worked in agribusiness for eleven years.
for + a period, since + a starting point. Never "I work here since".

items.situation: He asks: "When did you become legal manager?"
tips: There is a date, so the past simple wins.

items.situation: He asks: "Have you ever worked on a carbon project?"
tips: No, I have never worked on one, but I have read the regulation.
ever and never live with the present perfect.

items.situation: He asks: "What is the largest contract you have negotiated?"
tips: The largest one I have negotiated was a supply contract with a European buyer.
The question is present perfect; the answer with a date goes back to the past simple.

items.situation: He asks: "Have you signed off on the new policy yet?"
tips: Not yet. I have already read it, but I have not signed off on it.
already goes before the verb, yet goes at the end.

items.situation: He asks: "Why do you want to move into the carbon market?"
tips: Because I have spent eleven years on the contract side, and the regulation is where the work is going.
One long sentence, with a reason. Not four words.

listenings.text: Hi Amanda, this is Martin Reis from the legal team. Thanks for making time on Friday. I wanted to give you a heads up about the call so that nothing takes you by surprise. It is a conversation, not an interview, and it lasts about thirty minutes. I have read your profile already, so please do not repeat it line by line. What I am interested in is the story behind it: where you started, why you moved from the law firm to the company side, and what you have been doing since you took over the department. I will also ask about one contract that went wrong, because that is where I learn the most about a lawyer. And bring questions for me. Half of the call is yours. See you on Friday.

So, my name is Helena Duarte and this is the short version. I studied law in Porto Alegre and I joined a firm in my second year, which is where I learned to draft. I stayed for six years and I loved almost none of it, because I never met the client twice. In two thousand and seventeen I moved in-house, to a food company, and everything changed: suddenly I was in the room where the decision happened. I have been in-house ever since. I have worked on supply contracts, on two acquisitions and, for the last three years, on environmental compliance, which nobody in my team wanted and which turned out to be the most interesting work I have ever done. If you are thinking about the same move, my advice is simple. Go where the decision is made.

extra_audio.text: Start with where you are now and how long you have been there. Then go back to the beginning and say where you studied and where you started. Then say what you did in each step, with the dates. Then say what has changed since you took over the department. And finally, say what you want next and why.
